Making booze was a hobby of mine or years, and is now my job (mater distiller). Here's what I've learned from it.

Never cut corners: If you're going to do a job, do the job right. Plenty of ways to do a half ass job in this world, but if you want to make something great you don't cheat. There aren't any shortcuts that won't show in the finished product.

Be honest: Not only with other people, but with yourself. I've tasted terrible beers and spirits from people who were bullshitting themselves all day long. They lie to themselves about what they're making, and then try to sell the lie to you with a straight face.

Process matters: Make a list and check it twice. Bad luck happens, but accidents don't happen unless that bad luck intersects with bad planning and stupid mistakes. A good process keeps bad luck from ruining thousands o dollars of product.

Never whistle when you're pissing: You can do one thing at a time really well. If you try to do too many things at once, you're not going to be doing any of them to the best of your ability.

Happiness is loving your job: About twenty years ago, I was working an IT job. I would sit in the parking lot dreading to go in. At one point I asked myself "How much would somebody have to pay me to suck a dick rather than go in". When I realized I actually had a number for that question, I knew it was time to leave. A good job is one you would do even if you weren't being paid for it. I have that. I I won the lottery tomorrow, I would still do my job and invest that money into more equipment around here. That's a good life.

Unless you really, really, really, really love it; don't go to medical school. You can make a lot more money, with a lot less work, and abuse, doing anything else.

And chances are, in medicine, you still wont get to do what you want.

Ideas are dime-a-dozen and everybody has them.

What really matters is the ability to turn ideas into reality. If you don't have this ability you are just another bag of hot air.

Software development: It's not difficult but it is a completely different way of thinking. And if you're working hard, you're thinking all. day. long. And you come home exhausted. And not everyone can think in the way that programming needs. You need to be able to think in black and white. You need to be able to concentrate for long hours at a stretch.

That said, the pay is incredible.
This us what I'm in college for now, and I love the way you have to think to get stuff done. It just makes so much sense.

I use my hobbies as a time to relax and be creative. Most of the people who do the same hobbies as me (painting, jewelry making, and other forms of art) are much happier with it if they start the hobby because it's something they enjoy doing, rather than because they think they can make some money off of it. I do Quality assurance/control for a geophysical company. Basically I make sure all charts and figures coincide with the report and are aesthetically pleasing.

Know who you work with. Get to know everyone and approximately what they do on a day to day basis. It's good to know what their process is, so that you can understand where they are coming from and how they work, so that you don't wind up asking for things that frustrate them or make their job more complicated. Understanding how each individual prefers to be approached and how they work really goes a long way. I would say how you approach an individual matters more than what you are approaching them about. If you do not have a good relationship with your coworkers and your position requires you to correct people, you can create an awful work environment for everyone.

Just know how people like to be talked to. Treat them well and they will treat you well. Respect their job and they will respect yours.
